stages.title: Reading and writing fundamentals
stages.hook: Why do Turkish people say 'anne' with a doubled n and not like 'ane'?
explain: Turkish words are split into syllables, and every syllable has exactly one vowel: a-ğaç, ki-tap, an-ne. A double consonant is really said twice, so 'anne' is an-ne, with a slightly long n. This is why spelling matters: 'ala' and 'alla' are different.

When a word ending in p, ç, t or k gets a vowel ending, the last consonant often softens: kitap becomes kitabı (his book), ağaç becomes ağacı, and çocuk becomes çocuğu. When you write, say the word in syllables and listen for the doubled sounds.
stages.mnemonic: Break the word into beats: an-ne, ki-tap, çi-çek. One vowel, one beat.

gq.why: Each syllable has one vowel, and kitap has two vowels.
A written double consonant is pronounced as a longer or doubled sound.

panel.q: Why does 'kitap' become 'kitabı' in 'his book'?
o: Turkish changes every consonant before a suffix
The final p softens to b before a vowel
The word kitap is irregular and has two forms
The p is dropped and the vowel is lengthened
panel.why: Final p, ç, t, k often soften between vowels.

panel.q: Why is the silent ğ still written in 'dağ'?
o: It shows the word is foreign
It lengthens the vowel before it and is not said as a consonant
panel.why: Ğ is a letter in its own right but it is not pronounced as a consonant: it lengthens the vowel before it, so dağ sounds like a long 'daa'.

panel.q: Why does çiçek become çiçeği when an ending such as -i is added?
o: The word is spelled wrongly in the plural and should be çiçeki
Turkish has no letter k before a vowel in any word
All Turkish words change their last consonant to ğ
Final k softens to ğ before a vowel ending
panel.why: Çiçek + -i becomes çiçeği.

teach.model: Turkish words are split into syllables with one vowel each. Doubled letters are pronounced twice, like an-ne. Final p, ç, t, k soften to b, c, d, ğ before a vowel ending.

points.ask: How do you split a word?
What changes at the end of a word?

trip.prompt: Look for consonant softening on the page.

stages.title: Basic sentence construction
stages.hook: In English you say 'I eat bread'. How would you order those three words in Turkish?
explain: The Turkish sentence order is subject, object, verb: 'Ben ekmek yiyorum' (I bread eat). The verb is at the end. The word that gets the most attention can sit just before the verb. Turkish has no word for 'the' (bir is used for 'a' when needed), and it uses no separate verb 'to be' in the present with nouns: an ending does it.

To say 'I am a student', add -im to the noun: 'Ben öğrenciyim'. The endings are -im (I), -sin (you), nothing for he/she, -iz (we), -siniz (you all), -ler (they). With vowel harmony, they change shape: öğretmenim (I am a teacher), doktorum (I am a doctor).
stages.mnemonic: Subject first, object next, verb last: SOV.

gq.q: What is the usual word order in Turkish?
How do you say 'I am a doctor'?

panel.q: Why is 'Ben öğrenciyim' correct and 'Ben öğrenci' not natural for a full statement?
o: Turkish needs the word 'is' between the two nouns
Öğrenci is a verb, so it cannot stand alone
The ending -im marks the person 'I am'
The pronoun ben changes to benim in full statements
panel.why: The ending carries the meaning of 'to be'.

panel.q: Why do endings change shape, like -im, -ım, -um, -üm?
o: They are different words that all mean 'I am' in speech
The choice is random and depends on the speaker's region
They show whether the speaker is male or female
Vowel harmony makes the ending match the last vowel
panel.why: Four-way harmony adapts the ending to the stem vowel.

panel.q: Which version is natural for 'We are teachers'?
panel.why: -iz is the ending for 'we are'.

teach.model: The verb is at the end: subject, object, verb. 'To be' is an ending on the word: öğrenciyim (I am a student). There is no a or the.

trip.prompt: Look at the basic order of words in a Turkish sentence.

stages.title: Common verbs
stages.hook: Which verb ending tells you who is doing the action?
explain: Verbs appear in their basic form with -mek or -mak: gitmek (to go), gelmek (to come), okumak (to read), yazmak (to write), almak (to take or buy), vermek (to give), yapmak (to do or make). Drop -mek/-mak to find the stem.

Present continuous: stem + -iyor + person ending. gel + iyor + um = geliyorum (I am coming), oku + yor + sun = okuyorsun (you are reading). Vowels in -iyor change by harmony: yazıyorum (I am writing). The negative adds -me/-ma before it: gelmiyorum (I am not coming).
stages.mnemonic: Stem plus -yor plus who: geliyorum, geliyorsun, geliyor.

gq.why: Remove -mak to find the stem oku.

gq.q: How do you say 'I am not coming'?

panel.q: Why is it 'yazıyorum' and not 'yaziyorum'?
o: It is a typing mistake, because the i must always be dotted
Turkish dots every i, so yaziyorum is also correct
The ı is silent and only shows a longer a before it
Turkish uses ı and the vowel follows harmony
panel.why: After the stem vowel a, the harmonic vowel is ı.

panel.q: Which ending shows 'you' in the present continuous?
panel.why: The second person singular ending is -sin/-sun: okuyorsun.

panel.q: How would you show 'she is not writing'?
panel.why: Stem yaz + negative -mı + -yor, with no ending for 'she'.

teach.model: Verbs end in -mek or -mak. Remove it to find the stem, then add -iyor and the person ending. Add -me/-ma before for no.

points.ask: How do I find the stem?
How do I say 'I am doing'?

trip.prompt: Look at the table of the present continuous.

stages.title: Nouns, pronouns and modifiers
stages.hook: In Turkish you can say 'in the house' without a separate word for 'in'. How?
explain: Turkish glues small endings onto nouns. The plural is -ler/-lar: ev (house), evler (houses). Place endings: -de/-da (at, in): evde (at home); -den/-dan (from): evden (from home); -e/-a (to): eve (to the house).

Possession is also an ending: evim (my house), evin (your house), evi (his or her house). Pronouns are ben, sen, o, biz, siz, onlar. Adjectives come before the noun and do not change: büyük ev (big house), büyük evler (big houses). The order is stem, plural, possessive, case: evlerimde (in my houses).

gq.why: The ending -de means in or at.

panel.q: In what order do endings attach?
panel.why: Turkish noun suffixes follow plural, possessive, case: evlerimde.

panel.q: Why is 'okuldan' not 'okulden'?
o: Okul ends in a consonant, so it takes -den
The last vowel is u (back), so -dan is used
The word okul is irregular and takes -den
Okul is a verb here, so it takes a different ending
panel.why: Vowel harmony gives -dan after a back vowel.

panel.q: Which phrase means 'to the school'?
panel.why: The dative ending -a/-e means to.

teach.model: Turkish adds endings to a noun: ev, evler, evim, evde. Order: plural, possessive, case. Adjectives come before the noun and do not change.

points.ask: How does Turkish make new forms?
What order do endings go in?

trip.prompt: See how one word can carry many meanings.

stages.title: Questions and responses
stages.hook: How do you ask a yes/no question in Turkish without changing the word order?
explain: For yes/no questions, add the particle mi (mı, mu, mü) after the word you ask about, written separately: 'Sen öğrenci misin?' (Are you a student?). The particle takes a harmonic vowel and a personal ending: 'Kitap okuyor musun?'

Question words are ne (what), kim (who), nerede (where), nasıl (how), neden (why), kaç (how many) and hangi (which). They stay in the place where the answer would be: 'Okul nerede?' (Where is the school?). The answer: 'Okul orada.' (The school is there.) Short answers: evet (yes), hayır (no).
stages.mnemonic: Add mi after the thing you are unsure about.

gq.q: How do you make a yes/no question?
gq.why: The question particle mi follows the word being questioned.

panel.q: Which is correct: 'Okuyor musun?' or 'Okuyormusun?'
o: Okuyor mısın? (particle with the vowel ı)
panel.why: The particle is written separately in modern Turkish.

panel.q: Why is it 'Hazır mısınız?' and not 'Hazır mı siniz?'
o: Mı is a verb and takes the ending -siniz after it
Turkish forbids spaces before the ending -siniz
The personal ending attaches to the particle
The word hazır is foreign and keeps a separate ending
panel.why: The person ending is added to the question particle.

panel.q: Why is 'mı' used in 'Kapı açık mı?'
o: The particle is chosen at random and mı is the most common
Kapı is a verb, so it needs the question verb mı
Here mı means 'what' and not a question marker
Harmony: the last vowel ı needs mı
panel.why: The vowel in mi follows the last vowel of the preceding word.

teach.model: Use mi, mı, mu or mü for yes/no questions, written separately. Question words are ne, kim, nerede, nasıl, neden, kaç. They stay in the usual place.

trip.prompt: Study how yes/no questions are built.

stages.title: Describing people and places
stages.hook: Describe your best friend and your town in Turkish: which words do you need?
explain: Description uses adjectives before nouns and the ending for 'to be'. Useful adjectives: güzel (beautiful), büyük (big), küçük (small), yeni (new), eski (old), uzun (long or tall), kısa (short), iyi (good). 'Şehir güzel' means 'The city is beautiful'.

For 'there is' and 'there is not', Turkish uses var and yok: 'Parkta ağaç var' (There is a tree in the park), 'Evde su yok' (There is no water at home). People are described like this: 'Arkadaşım uzun ve güzel gözlü' (My friend is tall and has beautiful eyes) is more advanced. Start simple: 'O iyi biri' (She or he is a good person).
stages.mnemonic: Güzel, büyük, küçük: describe, then add var or yok.
sentences: There is a tree in the park.

gq.q: How do you say 'There is no water'?

gq.why: Eski is old; yeni is new.

panel.q: How do you say 'The house is big'?
panel.why: An adjective after the noun works as the predicate: Ev büyük. Büyük ev, with the adjective first, means 'a big house'.

panel.q: A friend says 'Parkta çocuk var'. What do you know?
o: The child is not in the park
There is a child in the park
panel.why: Var states existence; -ta marks location.

panel.q: Why is 'Evde su yok' not translated word for word as 'No water in the house is'?
o: Turkish has its own structure: place, thing, var or yok
Turkish never uses yok and says 'su değil' for 'no water'
It is a mistake: the sentence should say 'Su evde yoktur'
Su is a verb meaning 'to be absent' in this sentence
panel.why: The pattern place + noun + var/yok is natural.

teach.model: Use adjectives before nouns: büyük ev. Use var for there is and yok for there is not. Place goes first: Parkta ağaç var.

points.ask: How do I say there is?

trip.prompt: Study how adjectives and existence words work.

stages.title: Time, dates and daily routines
stages.hook: How do you ask 'What time is it?' in Turkish?
explain: Ask 'Saat kaç?' and the answer is 'Saat üç' (It is three o'clock). Half past is 'buçuk': saat üç buçuk. Days of the week: Pazartesi (Monday), Salı, Çarşamba, Perşembe, Cuma, Cumartesi, Pazar (Sunday). To say 'on Monday', use the days alone: Pazartesi günü or just Pazartesi.

Daily routine verbs use -iyor: 'Sabah yedide kalkıyorum' (I get up at seven in the morning). The ending -de/-da (-te/-ta) means 'at' a time. Morning is sabah, afternoon is öğleden sonra, evening is akşam and night is gece.
sentences: I go to school on Monday.

gq.q: How do you say 'half past two'?
gq.why: Buçuk means and a half after the hour.

panel.q: Why do we say 'yedide' for 'at seven'?
o: Yedi is a verb, so -de is its ending
It means 'from seven', as in 'from seven o'clock'
It means 'for seven days' in the same pattern
panel.why: The locative -de marks time and place.

panel.q: Which word is 'afternoon'?
panel.why: Öğleden sonra means after noon, i.e. afternoon.

panel.q: How do you ask the time politely?
panel.why: Saat kaç? is the standard way.

teach.model: Ask Saat kaç? and answer Saat üç. Add -de for at a time: yedide. The days are Pazartesi to Pazar.

stages.title: Food and shopping
stages.hook: Order tea at a Turkish café. What do you say?
explain: Ordering is short and polite: 'Bir çay lütfen' (One tea, please). Food words: ekmek (bread), su (water), peynir (cheese), çorba (soup), pilav (rice), simit (sesame bread ring), elma (apple), balık (fish). For prices, 'Ne kadar?' means 'How much?'.

The currency is lira (Türk lirası). A shop assistant may say 'Başka bir şey?' (Anything else?). You can answer 'Hepsi bu kadar' (That is all). Tea (çay) is served in small tulip-shaped glasses and is the national drink at home, work and cafés.
stages.mnemonic: Bir çay lütfen. Ne kadar? Teşekkürler.

gq.why: Başka bir şey means another thing, i.e. anything else.

panel.q: What does 'bir' do in 'Bir çay lütfen'?
panel.why: Bir is the number one and also the word for a.

panel.q: A waiter asks 'Başka bir şey?'. What is the natural 'no more' answer?
panel.why: It means 'That's all'.

panel.q: Which is the most natural polite order?
panel.why: Bir plus noun plus lütfen is the usual polite pattern.

teach.model: To order, say bir çay lütfen. Ask the price with Ne kadar? Say Hepsi bu kadar when finished.

points.ask: How do I ask the price?

stages.title: Everyday conversations
stages.hook: Imagine you meet a new classmate. Can you hold a short conversation?
explain: A simple conversation: 'Merhaba, benim adım Elif. Senin adın ne?' 'Benim adım Can. Memnun oldum.' 'Ben de memnun oldum. Nerelisin?' 'İstanbulluyum. Sen?' 'Ben İzmirliyim.' The suffix -li means 'from': Ankaralı (from Ankara).

Use 'Sen' with friends and 'Siz' with strangers or elders. Common helpers: 'Hoş geldiniz' (welcome), answered with 'Hoş bulduk'. 'Afiyet olsun' is said to someone who is about to eat or is eating. 'Geçmiş olsun' is said to someone who is ill or has had bad luck.

gq.q: Which suffix shows where someone is from?
What do you say to someone who says 'Hoş geldiniz'?
gq.why: Hoş bulduk is the standard reply.

panel.q: When do you say 'Afiyet olsun'?
o: When someone arrives at your home
When someone is ill or in hospital
When someone leaves the table for good
panel.why: It means 'may it be healthy' at meals.

panel.q: Why use 'Siz' with a new elderly neighbour?
panel.why: Siz is the polite form.

panel.q: A friend is unwell. Which phrase fits?
panel.why: It means 'may it pass'.

teach.model: Greet, ask the name with Adın ne?, ask Nerelisin?, say Memnun oldum. Use sen with friends and siz with elders or strangers.

points.ask: How do I ask the name?
How do I ask where from?
